circuit-breaker: A circuit-breaker is a mechanical [[switching-device]] capable of making, carrying and breaking currents under normal circuit conditions and also of making, carrying for a specified time and breaking currents under specified abnormal circuit conditions such as those of short-circuit ([[iec-56]] 3.102.3, IEV 441-14-20). It is the fundamental [[mechanical-switching-device]] of this standard, distinguished from simpler switches by its short-circuit interrupting duty. Its current-carrying path runs through the [[main-circuit]] of each [[pole]], where the [[main-contact]] carries continuous current and the [[arcing-contact]] takes the arc during interruption. Circuit-breakers are classified by arc-extinguishing medium and tank construction into the [[dead-tank-circuit-breaker]], [[live-tank-circuit-breaker]], [[air-circuit-breaker]], [[oil-circuit-breaker]], [[vacuum-circuit-breaker]], [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]], [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] variants. A [[restrike-free-circuit-breaker]] is one that meets defined no-restrike performance.
dead-tank-circuit-breaker: A dead tank circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which a vessel(s) at earth potential surrounds and contains the interrupter(s) and the insulating medium ([[iec-56]] 3.102.4, IEV 441-14-25). The defining characteristic is that the enclosing tank is held at earth (ground) potential, so the interrupting unit sits inside an earthed housing rather than being elevated on insulators. Bushings carry the conductors through the earthed tank to the line terminals. This contrasts directly with the [[live-tank-circuit-breaker]], where the interrupter enclosure is at line potential. The dead-tank construction is common where current transformers are mounted on the bushings and is typical of many oil and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] designs. Like all [[circuit-breaker]] types it carries continuous current through the [[main-contact]] and commutates the arc to the [[arcing-contact]] of each [[pole]].
live-tank-circuit-breaker: A live tank circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which a vessel(s) containing the interrupter(s) is at a potential above earth ([[iec-56]] 3.102.5, IEV 441-14-26). Its distinguishing feature is that the interrupter housing is energised at line potential and is supported on post-insulators that provide insulation to earth, so the tank itself is "live." This is the opposite arrangement to the [[dead-tank-circuit-breaker]], whose enclosure is at earth potential. Live-tank construction is lighter, uses less insulating medium, and is widely used for [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] designs at transmission voltages, often built up from a [[module]] stack per [[pole]]. Each pole conducts continuous current through its [[main-contact]] and transfers the arc to the [[arcing-contact]] during interruption.
air-circuit-breaker: An air circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the contacts open and close in air at atmospheric pressure ([[iec-56]] 3.102.6, IEV 441-14-27). The distinguishing feature is that interruption and the dielectric recovery occur in ordinary atmospheric-pressure air, typically aided by arc-control devices such as arc chutes and magnetic blow-out, rather than by a compressed gas blast or a liquid. It should not be confused with the [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] (3.102.11), which extinguishes the arc with a blast of compressed air, nor with the [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]] family. Air circuit-breakers are mainly used at lower and medium voltages. As with every [[circuit-breaker]], continuous current flows through the [[main-contact]] of each [[pole]], while the [[arcing-contact]] takes and clears the arc as the contacts separate.
oil-circuit-breaker: An oil circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the contacts open and close in oil ([[iec-56]] 3.102.7, IEV 441-14-28). The arc drawn between the separating contacts decomposes the surrounding oil, generating hydrogen-rich gas and pressure that cool and deionise the arc, so the oil is both the arc-extinguishing and the insulating medium. Designs range from bulk-oil types, frequently built as a [[dead-tank-circuit-breaker]], to minimum-oil types. It contrasts with the gas-interrupting [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]], [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]] and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]], and with the [[vacuum-circuit-breaker]] and [[air-circuit-breaker]]. Each [[pole]] carries rated current continuously through its [[main-contact]] and commutates the arc to the [[arcing-contact]] on opening, the arcing contact being sacrificial to protect the main contact from arc erosion.
vacuum-circuit-breaker: A vacuum circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the contacts open and close within a highly evacuated envelope ([[iec-56]] 3.102.8, IEV 441-14-29). Its distinguishing feature is that arc interruption takes place in a sealed vacuum interrupter, where the very low gas density gives rapid dielectric recovery and the arc, sustained only by metal vapour from the contacts, extinguishes at the first current zero. There is no gas or liquid arc-extinguishing medium, distinguishing it from the [[oil-circuit-breaker]], [[air-circuit-breaker]], [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]] and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]]. Vacuum technology is dominant in medium-voltage switchgear. As with any [[circuit-breaker]] [[pole]], rated current is carried continuously, the [[main-contact]] and [[arcing-contact]] functions here being combined within the single contact pair inside the vacuum bottle.
gas-blast-circuit-breaker: A gas-blast circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the arc is extinguished by a blast of gas ([[iec-56]] 3.102.9, IEV 441-14-30). The defining mechanism is a directed flow (blast) of gas across the arc that cools, lengthens and deionises it so that it cannot reignite at current zero. This is the generic parent category for blast-type interrupters: the [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] (3.102.11) uses compressed air as the blast gas, while the [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] (3.102.10) uses sulphur hexafluoride. It is distinct from the [[oil-circuit-breaker]], [[vacuum-circuit-breaker]] and atmospheric [[air-circuit-breaker]]. Like all [[circuit-breaker]] designs it conducts continuous current through the [[main-contact]] of each [[pole]] and directs the blast onto the [[arcing-contact]] as the contacts part.
sf6-circuit-breaker: A sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the arc is extinguished in sulphur hexafluoride gas ([[iec-56]] 3.102.10, IEV 441-14-31). SF6 is an electronegative gas with excellent arc-quenching and dielectric properties; it captures free electrons to give rapid dielectric recovery, allowing compact interrupters at the highest transmission voltages. It is a specific member of the [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]] family (3.102.9), paralleling the [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] which instead blasts compressed air. SF6 designs may be built as a [[dead-tank-circuit-breaker]] or [[live-tank-circuit-breaker]], the latter often a stacked [[module]] arrangement per [[pole]]. Each pole carries rated current through its [[main-contact]] and transfers the arc to the [[arcing-contact]], with the gas flow (puffer or self-blast) directed across the arc at separation.
air-blast-circuit-breaker: An air-blast circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] in which the arc is extinguished by a blast of compressed air ([[iec-56]] 3.102.11, IEV 441-14-32). The distinguishing feature is a high-pressure air reservoir that releases a powerful blast across the separating contacts at opening, cooling and deionising the arc for interruption at current zero; the same air often provides insulation and operating energy. It is a specific type of [[gas-blast-circuit-breaker]] (3.102.9) using air as the blast gas, the direct counterpart of the [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] which uses sulphur hexafluoride. It must not be confused with the [[air-circuit-breaker]] (3.102.6), where contacts simply open in atmospheric air without a blast. Each [[pole]] carries current through its [[main-contact]] and clears the arc on its [[arcing-contact]].
restrike-free-circuit-breaker: A restrike-free circuit-breaker is a [[circuit-breaker]] that interrupts without restrike during the capacitive current-breaking test duties specified in this standard ([[iec-56]] 3.102.12). Unlike the preceding entries this clause is defined verbatim in the body rather than by IEV reference. A "restrike" is a resumption of current between the contacts a quarter-cycle or more after interruption, which is especially troublesome when switching capacitive loads such as no-load lines, cables and capacitor banks because it can cause damaging voltage escalation. The term is a performance classification, not a construction type: any of the medium-based designs, the [[sf6-circuit-breaker]], [[vacuum-circuit-breaker]], [[air-blast-circuit-breaker]] or [[oil-circuit-breaker]], may qualify if it passes the capacitive switching tests without restriking. Performance still depends on each [[pole]] and its [[arcing-contact]] behaviour.
pole: A pole of a circuit-breaker is the portion associated exclusively with one electrically separated conducting path of the main circuit and excluding those portions which provide a means for mounting and operating all poles together ([[iec-56]] 3.103.1, IEV 441-15-01). In a three-phase [[circuit-breaker]] there is one pole per phase, each being an electrically independent unit through which one line conductor passes. A pole contains the relevant [[main-circuit]] conducting path, including its [[main-contact]] and [[arcing-contact]], and, in higher-voltage designs, may be built up from one or more [[module]] assemblies stacked in series. The number of poles is a basic rating of the breaker. Poles are commonly operated together by a common mechanism, the shared mounting and operating means being explicitly excluded from the pole itself.
main-circuit: The main circuit is all the conductive parts of a circuit-breaker included in the circuit which it is designed to close and open ([[iec-56]] 3.103.2, IEV 441-15-02). It is the principal current-carrying path through each [[pole]], comprising the terminals, conductors and contacts that make and break the load and fault current, as distinct from the auxiliary and control circuits (3.103.3, 3.103.4) which serve signalling and operating functions and do not normally carry the main current. Within the main circuit the [[main-contact]] (3.103.7) carries the continuous current in the closed position, while the [[arcing-contact]] (3.103.8) is the part on which the arc is established during interruption. The main circuit thus defines the power-frequency conducting path whose making, carrying and breaking capacity is the essential duty of the [[circuit-breaker]].
main-contact: A main contact is a contact included in the main circuit of a circuit-breaker, intended to carry, in the closed position, the current of the main circuit ([[iec-56]] 3.103.7, IEV 441-15-07). Its function is to provide the low-resistance, continuous current-carrying path through each [[pole]] of the [[main-circuit]]. The main contact is paired with and protected by the [[arcing-contact]] (3.103.8): on opening, the main contacts part first while the current commutates to the arcing contacts, so that arcing and the resulting erosion occur on the sacrificial arcing contact rather than on the main contact; on closing the sequence reverses. This division of duty preserves the low contact resistance and current rating of the main contact over many operations. It is one of the defined contact types (3.103.5) of a [[circuit-breaker]].
arcing-contact: An arcing contact is a contact on which the arc is established ([[iec-56]] 3.103.8, IEV 441-15-08). It is provided in the [[main-circuit]] of each [[pole]] specifically to take the arc during making and breaking, thereby protecting the [[main-contact]] (3.103.7) from arc erosion. In operation the arcing contacts are arranged to part after the main contacts on opening and to touch before them on closing, so the current transfers to the arcing contacts before the gap that arcs is created. Because they bear the thermal and erosive stress of arcing, arcing contacts are typically made of arc-resistant material (such as a tungsten alloy) and are renewable. They work together with the breaker's arc-control device (3.103.17) and the arc-extinguishing medium, and are a defined contact type (3.103.5) of the [[circuit-breaker]].
module: A module (of a pole of a circuit-breaker) is an assembly which generally comprises making or breaking units, post-insulators and mechanical parts and which is mechanically and electrically connected to other identical assemblies to form a pole of a circuit-breaker ([[iec-56]] 3.103.22). This clause is given verbatim in the body. A module is the repeatable building block from which a high-voltage [[pole]] is constructed: identical modules are stacked and connected in series to reach the required voltage rating. Each module incorporates one or more (making or breaking) units (3.103.21), the post-insulators that support and insulate it, and the associated mechanical parts. The concept is characteristic of modular [[live-tank-circuit-breaker]] and [[sf6-circuit-breaker]] designs, where building a pole from standard modules lets one design span a range of system voltages. The complete [[circuit-breaker]] comprises one such pole per phase.
